Key facts: no criminalisation of same-sex conduct or gender expression. Anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation in employment, goods and services, education, housing, health care (2010), expanded 2020. Hate crime law covering gender identity (2013). No marriage/civil unions. Constitution Article 18 removal of SO/GI in 2016 (symbolic). Social attitudes: hostile survey figures — 9.3% would accept an LGBT person as family doctor (2022), 56% say homosexuals shouldn't show preferences publicly (2010), 55% of youth wouldn't want homosexual neighbours (2015). Violence: 10 bias-motivated cases against trans people logged by community group in a year — raw count, no denominator, can't be compared. Enforcement uneven; complaints slow.

Note the "deliberately not counted" bit — no LGR info, which per rubric is not to be deducted.

So this is a middle-of-the-road case. No trans-specific criminalisation, no documented police targeting of trans visitors, no facility bans (not documented), no custody placement rule documented. There's a functioning anti-discrimination law but uneven enforcement; a hate-crime law covering GI; social hostility documented (tier 3-ish: societal hostility with thin-ish recourse). But wait, the survey figures are about "homosexuals"/LGB generally, and mainly dated. The 2022 9.3% figure is about LGBT person as family doctor — this is about LGBT broadly, not trans-specific, and it's a social-attitude measure rather than the behaviour being rated (service refusal in a traveller setting). Per rule 17, prevalence numbers must be about trans people specifically and the behaviour being rated. So this is a weak signal.

There's no documented trans-specific violence pattern with denominators, no state targeting, no universal-exposure measure documented.

Compare to anchors: 0.65 tier (Avalet etc.) — lawful expression, border accepts foreign passports, functioning service protections with demonstrated compliance, some awkwardness. This dossier has: no criminalisation, but no documented border practice for trans visitors (open question), no documented facility rules, anti-discrimination law covering goods and services but uneven enforcement, social attitudes quite hostile (much worse than 0.65 anchors where "most people regard gender diversity as unusual rather than dangerous"). Here 9.3% would accept an LGBT family doctor, 55% of youth wouldn't want homosexual neighbours — that's more like social hostility / strong disapproval. Article 18 removal, opposition campaigning against LGBT in schools. No same-sex partnership recognition — resident-facing, not counted, though the "trans visitor whose relationship would be classified as same-sex" has no route to recognition — that's a resident-facing/partner issue, not really a trans traveller exposure.

Hmm. So what tier? There's no documented universal-exposure practice (no bathroom ban, no custody rule, no border document friction documented). The documented negatives: societal hostility (tier 3-ish but with a thin recourse), slow complaint handling. The violence figure: 10 cases in a year, no denominator — treat as undocumented per rule 16.

Rule 20: activist visibility is not danger. Local discrimination and rejection in family/employment isn't the traveller sphere.

So this is essentially: no trans-specific legal exposure, thin/open border and facility picture, functioning anti-discrimination law with uneven enforcement, latent social conservatism. Per rule 13, a jurisdiction with no trans-specific offence, no documented targeting, but no documented social acceptance sits below acceptance-with-protections tier — a step, not a tier.

Compared to 0.55 anchors: Isvera (recurring identity-based refusals in hotels/cafés, slow remedies), 0.65 anchors have documented acceptance and working remedies.

This dossier documents no trans-visitor-specific harm; it documents general LGB social conservatism and a legal framework that's protective on paper with uneven enforcement. The absence of documented trans-visitor incidents in a country with a functioning-ish civil society and UN visit — moderately positive but the dossier is somewhat thin on trans specifically.

I'd place around 0.55–0.60. Rule 3: absence of documented incidents — in a well-documented state, silence is a moderately positive signal. There is a UN visit and an annual review, so it's reasonably documented. Undocumented trans-specific malice.

But social hostility is real and documented: high levels of disapproval of homosexuality, opposition political messaging. Rule 19: is that friction or hostility? "should not show preferences in public" and "would not want homosexual neighbours" — disapproval/moral objection, social friction to hostility border. Not framed as threat/deceiver typically by the state. The Article 18 removal and the lawmaker calling homosexuality a disease is state-adjacent hostility but symbolic/verbal.

I think ~0.55 is defensible: no criminalisation, existing anti-discrimination coverage, hate-crime law, but hostile social climate and uneven enforcement, plus unresolved border/facility/custody picture. Maybe 0.60 since no documented trans-specific targeting or facility exclusion at all, unlike 0.55 anchors which had documented recurring service refusals. Here the violence is 10 logged cases, which is a small number (positive-ish signal in a country of a few million?), though no denominator.

Hmm — 10 bias-motivated cases against trans people in a year is not negligible but is a raw count. Per rule 16 it can't be used as magnitude. Treated as undocumented.

I'll say 0.58–0.60. Let me pick 0.58. Actually let's consider whether the hostile social climate should push lower. The 0.45 tier involves a universal unremedied exposure (facility ban, transport searches, ward rules, widespread discrimination survey). None documented here. The 0.55 tier is "repeated visitor-facing harms or incomplete remedies" — arguably the incomplete remedy (one of nine cases concluded; nine-month delay) plus general hostility. So 0.55 seems apt.
